President Donald Trump’s administration’s unprecedented and unpredictable gambles in foreign policy endeavours—the withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal, a policy of rapprochement towards North Korea, and renegotiation of crucial trade deals with global powers—places Canada at inconvenient crossroads. This begs the following question:

Since Trump’s inauguration in 2016, joint partnerships and policies surrounding trade, mobility, and continental security have been imposed and dictated upon Canada—not discussed. On the insistence of the United States, Canada joined the NATO training mission in Iraq in 2018. By Trump’s directives, Canada reluctantly agreed to renegotiate NAFTA with the United States and Mexico. While President Trump vociferously complained about illegal migration into the U.S. from other countries, Canada quietly processed thousands of unlawful refugees traversing the United States onto the Canadian side of the border.

While President Trump has openly called Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau “dishonest and weak” and “two-faced” after their encounters at the G7 Summit in Quebec and the NATO Leaders Summit in London, respectively, the Canadian government has opted to maintain a policy of silence in response. Not because we are somehow inherently superior in culture, tolerance, or attitude, but because the Trudeau government is afraid to trade diatribes with an unpredictable and impulsive president who has threatened some of his closest allies with sanctions and economic pressure in the past.

According to Randolph Mank, a former diplomat and research fellow at the Balsillie School of International Affairs, the focal point of Canadian foreign policy has been “to obtain a seat on the UN Security Council, though it’s unclear what we hope to achieve with it.” By exclusively focusing on the dissemination of some of our values surrounding climate change, feminist ideology, and multiculturalism, Canada is merely amplifying its domestic priorities outwards while other pressing geostrategic issues are flouted.

A wide range of domestic issues in Canada—ranging from the political perils of a minority Parliament, coupled with the growing power of separatists in Parliament, Indigenous rights movements, and the disenfranchisement of Western provinces with federalism—have overshadowed the foreign policy portfolio. Without doubt, reaching a mutually agreeable resolution in concert with various domestic political stakeholders armed with a long list of grievances is an arduous task for a minority Parliament. At the same time, the Trudeau government’s singular focus on resolving domestic affairs by negligently subjugating the creation of a comprehensive foreign policy enterprise is not only irresponsible but also unbecoming for Canada as a liberal democratic state.

Aside from bandwagoning on to the U.S. foreign policy train, there is an urgent need for a foreign policy review in Ottawa to clarify and promulgate our stance on crucial issues, including but not limited to, active commitment to NATO missions, disarmament, peace negotiations, and trade.
